easy.heading: Waking Up With A Gentle Start
easy.body:
Hey there! Grab a mug and let us talk about today's Pips. The easy puzzle today felt like a nice warm hug. I started right at the top where there was a sum of 12 for the cells at 0,3 and 0,4. Since the biggest number on any domino is a 6, the only way to get 12 is to have two 6s side by side. I looked at my dominoes and saw that only two had a 6 on them: the 0,6 and the 5,6. That gave me a huge head start.

Once I knew those 6s had to be there, I looked at the dominoes connected to them. Since 0,3 was a 6, it had to be part of the 0,6 domino, which placed the 0 in cell 0,2. That was perfect because the equals constraint for 0,1 and 0,2 meant that 0,1 also had to be a 0. From there, the rest of the puzzle just fell into place. I finished up by placing the 4,0 and 5,0 dominoes near the bottom to satisfy that tricky sum of 0 and the sum of 5 in the corner. It was a really satisfying way to kick off the morning.
easy.tips: Try looking for the highest and lowest sum targets first. A sum of zero or a very high sum like 12 usually only has one possible combination of numbers, which helps you lock down those dominoes instantly.

medium.heading: Stepping Up The Game In The Middle
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today was a bit of a step up, but it was still totally manageable if you kept your cool. The big breakthrough for me was looking at the greater than constraints. Specifically, the cell at 2,2 had to be greater than 5. In the world of dominoes, that is a fancy way of saying it has to be a 6. Looking at our list, the 2,6 and 4,6 were the candidates, but the 2,6 worked perfectly with the equals region next to it.

I also spent a bit of time staring at the center where three cells all had to be equal at 1,3, 1,4, and 2,4. When you see a three-way tie like that, it really limits your options. I used the 5,3 domino across the middle to bridge the gap and then matched up the doubles where they fit best. The bottom empty cell at 3,0 was a nice anchor point to help me decide which way to flip the 1,0 domino. It is all about those little connections.
medium.tips: When you see an equals region that spans across three different cells, look at your available dominoes for numbers that appear most frequently. Those numbers are usually the ones that will fill up those large identical zones.

hard.heading: A Real Test Of Patience For The Finale
hard.body:
Wow, the hard puzzle today really made me work for it! The absolute key was that massive equals region right in the middle involving cells like 2,5, 2,6, 3,5, and 3,6. Because 3,5 and 3,6 are part of the same domino and they are in an equals region, that domino had to be a double. I looked at the 5,5 and the 2,2 and realized the 5,5 was the only one that made the surrounding sums work out. Once I committed to that whole area being 5s, the puzzle started to open up.

I did hit a bit of a wall with the sum of 7 in the top left corner. It took me a minute to realize how to distribute the pips across those four cells using the 0,1 and 0,3 dominoes. The breakthrough moment was realizing that the empty cells are basically zeros. By using those empty spots as gaps, I could navigate the 0,4 and 3,2 dominoes into the tight spaces near the bottom. It felt like a giant game of Tetris, but once that last domino, the 3,6, slid into place, everything clicked. If you got stuck on this one, don't worry, it was a tough nut to crack!
hard.tips: Don't be afraid to temporarily place a domino just to see how it affects the nearby sums. If you find a double domino and an equals region, they are almost always meant for each other.

explanation.learned: I learned that large equals regions are actually your best friend in the harder levels because they narrow down your choices so quickly. I also realized that looking at the remaining dominoes is just as important as looking at the board; sometimes you can solve a section just by seeing which domino is the only one left that fits a specific number.

faqs.question: How do you solve the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You solve it by placing the provided dominoes on the grid so that all the pips match the constraints like sums, equals, or greater than signs. Each domino is used exactly once.

faqs.question: What does the empty region mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty region constraint means that the cell must have zero pips in it. It is a great starting point for placing dominoes that have a zero on one side.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be rotated in the Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can flip and rotate the dominoes in any direction as long as they fit into the designated grid spaces and follow the mathematical rules of the regions.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for Hard Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: Start by identifying any double dominoes and seeing if they fit into equals regions. Then, look for high sum targets or constraints that only have one possible solution to create an anchor on the board.

faqs.question: Are Pips puzzles the same every day?
faqs.answer: The rules stay the same, but the grid shape, domino set, and mathematical constraints change daily. The difficulty levels range from Easy to Hard to provide a variety of challenges.
